title: Sixty-One Fires
passage:
Among the operations in the county that dry grain for money, the mixed-flow has a fixed reputation: the tall machine with the ducts inside is the one that burns. This is not folklore. Across nine harvests the fire department’s log records sixty-one dryer fires. Forty-four were in mixed-flow machines, which account for a third of the county’s drying capacity. The explanation is as settled as the count. A mixed-flow dryer walks grain down past staggered rows of inverted-V ducts, and the ducts collect fines – chaff, husk and broken kernel – which sit in hot air and eventually smolder. Clean the ducts weekly, the advice runs, or buy a cross-flow machine and stop worrying.

Ambrose Calverend, an engineer who spent two winters with those sixty-one files for a growers’ cooperative, thinks the count is right and the reason is wrong. The first thing he found was dirt. His team swabbed the duct faces of twenty-six machines that had never burned; per square foot the mixed-flow dryers carried what the cross-flow columns carried, within a few percent. The second was the clock. Burner controllers on thirty-eight machines had kept a data log. In the twenty-nine fires he could time, ignition came after the run was over – a median of forty minutes after the fan stopped. “What I will defend is the timing,” he says. “Why mixed-flow machines dominate the count is a softer argument, and I think it is about who buys them rather than what is inside them.” A mixed-flow costs enough that it goes to operations drying for their neighbors as well as themselves, at so much per ton per point of moisture, and those operations run late and shut down hot.

The firm that builds most of the county’s mixed-flow machines was unmoved. Delphine Grendisham, who runs its service department and has pulled fines out of ducts for eleven years, says the clock is the weak joint in the argument. A controller log ends when the machine stops. The other time in the file is the moment the call came in. On an unmanned site at two in the morning, that is when somebody looked out of a window, not when anything caught. “Set those two numbers side by side and of course the fire looks late,” she says. “It looks late because nobody was there to see it early.” The swabs she reads differently: her crews still pull buckets of fines in February from machines that swabbed clean in September.

Garrick Steadgrove, an economist at the growers’ mutual that writes most of the county’s dryer coverage, accepts the swabs and rejects nearly everything else. Cleaning has sold a great many service contracts, he says, and prevented, so far as he can measure, nothing. On that much he and Calverend agree, which puts him across the table from Grendisham, whose buckets he considers beside the point even when they are full. What he will not have is the shutdown. Sort the same sixty-one fires by date rather than by machine, he argues, and the machine stops mattering. Forty-nine fall in a nine-day stretch at the tail of each harvest, when the deduction schedule bites hardest and the elevator’s delivery window is closing. Custom operations work through the tail because that is when the work is there, which is why their machines fill the log. “Calverend has moved the cause from the machine to the shutdown,” Steadgrove says. “I would move it one step further out, to the contract – and then it stops being an engineering problem.”

The swabs are hard to walk past. The county’s standard advice rests on a difference in dirt that twenty-six machines failed to show, and nobody in the argument now defends it on the old ground. The clock is another matter. Grendisham’s objection has not been answered, and it cannot be answered from files like these; it needs a probe inside a machine that later burns, and nobody has one. Until then Calverend’s account fits the evidence without having been tested by it. What the mutual has to settle before next harvest is narrower. His remedy is nearly free – run the fan on for twenty minutes after the burner cuts – while Steadgrove’s is not the mutual’s to give, since the deduction schedule belongs to the elevators. Whether writing a run-on clause into next year’s policies would be worth anything turns on something nobody has worked out how to check. What does an operator do at two in the morning on the eighth day of a wet harvest, with trucks waiting and no one there to watch?
– Meredith Ockendale

The passage opens by conceding that the trade’s rule of thumb is arithmetically right – forty-four of sixty-one fires in mixed-flow machines that hold a third of capacity – and then spends four paragraphs on a three-way quarrel about the reason: fines in the ducts (Grendisham), the hot shutdown (Calverend), the harvest calendar and the deduction schedule (Steadgrove). D names both halves, the surviving pattern and the unsettled cause, without picking a winner. A is outside knowledge dressed in passage furniture: charges per ton per moisture point are mentioned once, but no price history is given and none is argued about. B is the scope error – the difficulty of dating a fire on an unmanned site is Grendisham’s single objection in paragraph three, a vivid sub-point promoted to main topic, and it borrows the coda’s ‘no one there to watch’ to feel central. C is a title-plausible theme the text never argues; custom drying appears only as an explanation of who owns mixed-flow machines, never as a practice anyone recommends against.

Hardly a fire in the log fell outside that stretch.
The mutual could slow the rush by rewriting the deduction schedule.

questions.rationale: One-inch inference from Steadgrove’s paragraph. He says the machine stops mattering once the fires are sorted by date, that forty-nine of sixty-one fall in the nine-day tail, that the deduction schedule bites hardest and the delivery window is closing then, and that custom dryers keep working through it because that is when the work is. What follows, one step out, is that the squeeze in those days is common to everyone drying, not a property of any particular machine – which is exactly why he wants the cause moved to the contract. B is the miscount, softened but not repaired: forty-nine of sixty-one leaves twelve fires outside the stretch, one in five of the log, and the passage keeps them in view by giving the total twice – ‘hardly a fire’ is exactly the rounding a hurried reader performs. C is the policy leap, and it also puts the lever in the wrong hands: the writer disposes of that remedy as not the mutual’s to give, since the deduction schedule belongs to the elevators. The mutual could not rewrite it if it wanted to. D is a plausible-sounding capacity claim the text never makes; the trucks waiting outside belong to the coda’s hypothetical night, not to a stated backlog.

questions.prompt: What is the writer’s attitude toward Calverend’s explanation?

options.text: She thinks the objections raised against it have now been met.
She stays out of it and leaves the reader to decide.
She thinks it fits the facts but has not been tested.
She is convinced enough to want his remedy written into next year’s policies.

questions.rationale: The final paragraph is the writer speaking in her own voice, and she says two things about Calverend’s account. It fits: the swabs are hard to walk past, the county’s standard advice rests on a difference in dirt that twenty-six machines failed to show, and nobody now defends that advice on the old ground. And it has not been tested: Grendisham’s objection has not been answered, it cannot be answered from files like these, and answering it would need a probe inside a machine that later burns, which nobody has. C states both halves in her own terms – it fits the facts, and it has not been tested. A is the measured overclaim, and what tempts is that one objection really is dead: the old ground for the fines explanation has no defenders left. The live one is not, and the paragraph says so twice over – ‘Grendisham’s objection has not been answered, and it cannot be answered from files like these …’ A reader who slides from the retired objection to the objections generally picks A. B is the neutral-reporter misread; a writer who calls one account untested, records that nobody defends the old advice any longer, and disposes of a third party’s remedy as something the mutual has no power to grant has not stayed out of it. D turns her verdict into a recommendation she declines to make. She does say the remedy is nearly free, and she does dispose of the rival remedy as not the mutual’s to give, which together make D feel like where the piece is heading; the very next sentence refuses it – ‘Whether writing a run-on clause into next year’s policies would be worth anything turns on something nobody has worked out how to check’ – and the piece ends on that question rather than on an answer. Note for the hedge audit: D carries a scoped qualifier of its own (‘convinced enough to’), so ‘pick the measured-sounding one’ still does not isolate the key here.
